title: Airflow Builder
description: This is a route-drawing puzzle on a mostly empty 64x64 board where a round ball token sits at a start spot and a cup-shaped goal sits somewhere else behind walls. The player builds the path by clicking cells in sequence: the first click selects the current open nozzle, the second click chooses where the next straight airflow segment should end, and if the line between them is clear a one-cell-thick strip of arrow tiles appears connecting those points. Every new segment must continue from the end of the previous one, so the board gradually fills with a visible chain of air corridors that show exactly how the ball will travel. Pressing SPACE launches the ball, which then moves cell by cell along the drawn arrows until it reaches the cup or crashes into a wall, in which case the level flashes an error. Level 1 should be an open board with one simple bend so the drawing rule is obvious, while later levels should add thin wall mazes, longer routing, and one level where the ball must be guided through a glowing ring before entering the cup. The challenge should come from planning the geometry of the drawn airflow, not from hidden rules or fast timing.

title: Mirror Shot
description: This is a fixed-screen beam-routing puzzle where a bright emitter sits on one edge of the board, a crystal target sits somewhere else, and the playfield contains a small number of square mirror sockets drawn as framed tiles. Clicking a socket rotates the mirror inside it between the two diagonal states, so the player can visibly change whether that tile reflects the beam like a slash or a backslash. Pressing SPACE fires a straight laser from the emitter, and the beam then travels across the board, bouncing off mirrors until it either hits the crystal and wins or hits a wall and stops. Level 1 should use just one mirror in a clean empty room so the reflection rule is learned instantly from the shot itself. Later levels should add more sockets, solid blocker tiles, and one level where two crystals are present but only one is active, forcing the player to read the target marker before arranging the path. Keep the whole board static and fully visible so the puzzle is about understanding line reflection and mirror orientation rather than navigation.

title: Ice Stop
description: This is a sliding movement puzzle viewed from above on a frozen room where the player controls a puck-like token with WASD. Whenever the player presses a direction, the puck should keep sliding in that direction across the light-blue ice until it hits a wall, a post, or another solid obstacle, and only then can the next input matter. The goal is a clearly marked dock tile, and the whole challenge is to stop in the right places so that each long slide lines up the next one. Level 1 should be a tiny room with a single turn so the player immediately sees that movement is all-or-nothing on ice. Later levels should introduce isolated stop-posts in the middle of the floor, longer rectangular chambers, and one level where a collectible star must be touched before sliding onto the dock counts as success. The visual design should make the slippery floor, hard walls, and stopping objects extremely legible so the game reads as momentum control rather than a normal maze.

title: Size Gates
description: This is a form-switching navigation puzzle where the player controls a solid square avatar that can be either a small 1x1 tile or a large 3x3 block, with SPACE switching between the two forms whenever there is enough room. The board should make the size rule visible through architecture: narrow one-cell tunnels that only the small form can enter, wide pressure plates that are clearly meant to be covered by the large form, and door frames whose openings visually match only one of the two body sizes. The player still moves with WASD, but the interesting choice is when to change form rather than how to route through a complicated maze. Level 1 should be extremely direct, with one narrow passage that forces the player to shrink before reaching the exit arch. Later levels should combine small tunnels with large floor plates that permanently open colored gates, so progress depends on using the right body shape at the right place. The grid should stay uncluttered and geometric so the player can read the puzzle just by comparing the avatar’s current footprint to the visible openings in the environment.

title: Claw Lanes
description: This is a side-view grab puzzle where the player does not move a character through the room directly, but instead controls a small crane carriage that rides left and right along a rail at the very top of the board. Pressing left or right shifts the carriage horizontally, and pressing SPACE drops a hanging claw straight down until it hits the floor, an obstacle, or a prize token, after which it retracts automatically along the same vertical line. The level is solved when the claw tip touches the glowing prize, so the player’s job is to choose the correct vertical lane from which to drop rather than to navigate in free space. Level 1 should be a simple open shaft with one visible prize directly below one possible rail position. Later levels should add tall pillars that block some drop lanes, roof overhangs that make certain columns useless, and one level where the player must first grab a key token that causes a locked barrier to vanish before the final prize becomes reachable. The whole screen should look like a small crane toy machine drawn in clean silhouette, so the puzzle is about reading vertical access lanes and blocked shafts at a glance.
